title: ITD 256 Midterm Review
description: Database concepts, the relational model and keys, SQL you actually run, ERD and Crow's Foot notation, and normalization.

sections.name: Database Concepts, File Systems & Data Models

questions.question: Match each basic file-system term to its definition.

pairs.right: Raw facts, with little meaning until organized
A character or group of characters with a specific meaning
A logically connected set of fields describing one person, place or thing
A collection of related records, in a non-DBMS system
A collection of related records, inside a DBMS

questions.explanation: File and Table have the same definition — the name changes depending on whether you're in a file-based system or a DBMS.

questions.question: Each file-system term has a database equivalent. Match them.

pairs.right: Attribute
Entity instance
Entity

questions.explanation: Field = attribute, record = entity instance, table = entity. These pairs come up constantly once you start drawing ERDs.

questions.question: Databases can be classified by the degree of structure in their data. Match each level to its description.

pairs.right: Data exists in its original, raw state
Data results from formatting, applied to suit a type of processing
Data that has been partially processed — XML, for instance

questions.explanation: XML is the standard example of semistructured data: it represents data elements in a textual format without imposing a full relational structure.

questions.question: The practical significance of data dependence is the difference between the logical and physical format. Which describes the LOGICAL format?
options: How the data is actually stored on the hardware
How the data is represented to the application or user
The order blocks are written to disk
The compression algorithm applied to the file
questions.explanation: Logical = the representation to the application or user. Physical = actual storage on hardware, which should be hidden completely and of no concern to the user.

questions.question: Unnecessarily storing the same data at different places is called data ______.
questions.explanation: Data redundancy. It creates "islands of information" and raises the odds of different versions of the same data existing at once.

questions.question: Match each anomaly to what goes wrong.

pairs.right: Changed data ends up inconsistent or incomplete
New data cannot be recorded completely
Removing one fact partially removes another

questions.explanation: These three are the reason normalization exists — they all come from putting facts about different things in the same table.

questions.question: Which DBMS function stores the definitions of data elements and their relationships?
questions.explanation: Data dictionary management. The data dictionary stores definitions of data elements and their relationships.

questions.question: SQL stands for ______ Query Language.
questions.explanation: Structured Query Language — the de facto query language and data access standard, supported by nearly all DBMS vendors with slight variations.

questions.question: Match each of the four basic building blocks of a data model to its definition.

pairs.right: A person, place, thing or event about which data is collected
A characteristic of an entity
An association among entities
A restriction placed on data to ensure integrity

questions.explanation: Entity, attribute, relationship, constraint — memorize these four; every ERD question is built out of them.

questions.question: When translating business rules into data model components, nouns generally become ______ and verbs generally become ______.
questions.explanation: Nouns translate into entities, verbs translate into relationships among entities.

questions.question: Relationships are always bidirectional — you have to read them from both ends.
questions.explanation: Because relationships run both ways, you ask two questions: how many B relate to one A, and how many A relate to one B.

questions.question: The relational model is based on the relation, which is another name for:
questions.explanation: A relation is a table or entity — a matrix of intersecting tuples (rows) and attributes (columns).

questions.question: What does an RDBMS do that the raw relational model does not?
options: It eliminates the need for primary keys
It hides the complexities of the relational model from the user and makes it easier to implement
It removes the need for any data model at all
It converts the database into a file system
questions.explanation: An RDBMS performs the basic functions of earlier DBMS types while making the relational model easier to understand and implement, hiding its complexities.

questions.question: Which pair correctly separates the logical model from the physical model?
options: Logical: what data is stored and how it relates. Physical: how it is actually implemented and stored
Logical: disk layout. Physical: business rules
Logical: only used after the database is built. Physical: only used in planning
They are two names for the same diagram
questions.explanation: Logical describes the structure as the user sees it; physical describes the actual implementation. The same distinction as logical vs physical format under data independence.

questions.question: A key is one or more attributes that ______ other attributes.
questions.explanation: Keys determine other attributes. That single word is what connects keys to normalization.

questions.question: Match each kind of primary key to its description.

pairs.right: A real-world identifier already familiar to end users
A made-up, artificial value such as an auto-number
A primary key built from more than one attribute

questions.explanation: A natural key is part of the day-to-day business vocabulary; a surrogate key exists only to be a key.

questions.question: Every table row must have a primary key.
questions.explanation: Each table row must have a primary key. That is entity integrity.

questions.question: Match each integrity rule to its requirement.

pairs.right: All primary key entries are unique, and no part of a primary key may be null
A foreign key is either null, or matches a primary key value in the related table

questions.explanation: Entity integrity governs the primary key of a row; referential integrity governs the foreign key pointing at another row.

questions.question: The absence of any data value in a column is called a ______.
questions.explanation: A null. It can mean an unknown value, a known but missing value, or an inapplicable condition.

questions.question: Match each catalogue-style term to what it actually describes.

pairs.right: A description of all tables in the database, created by the user and designer
A system data dictionary describing all objects in the database
The complete logical view — the full description of the database
The description of one individual table

questions.explanation: Note the distinction: the database schema covers everything; a relational schema is per-table.

questions.question: How is a many-to-many relationship implemented in a relational database?
options: By putting a foreign key in whichever table is larger
By creating a new connecting entity in 1:M relationships with both original entities
By merging the two tables into one
By storing a comma-separated list of key values in one column
questions.explanation: A new connecting entity — a bridge/composite/associative entity — sits between them in two 1:M relationships.

questions.question: What does a composite (bridge) entity contain?
options: The primary keys of the tables being linked, held as foreign keys
Copies of every attribute from both linked tables
Nothing — it is a view, not a table
questions.explanation: It includes the primary keys of the tables to be linked, as foreign keys — and together those usually form its composite primary key.

questions.question:
A firm needs to record which EMPLOYEEs work on which PROJECTs. An employee may be assigned many projects, and a project may have many employees.

Someone tries to do it with only the two main tables, each carrying a foreign key to the other:

• EMPLOYEE (emp_id, proj_id) — employee 1 works on projects 1, 2 and 3, so their proj_id has to read "1,2,3"
• PROJECT (proj_id, emp_id) — project 2 has employees 1, 2 and 3, so its emp_id has to read "1,2,3"

Why does this design not work?
options: Because foreign keys are not allowed in more than one table
Because a single foreign key field would have to hold several key values at once, violating the atomic attribute rule
Because the two tables would then have the same primary key
Because a table may not have more than two foreign keys
questions.explanation: One column holds one value. Writing "1,2,3" into proj_id breaks atomicity, and the same problem appears from the other direction in PROJECT — which is why an M:N needs a third table instead.

questions.question:
The M:N between EMPLOYEE and PROJECT is resolved with a bridge table, ASSIGNMENT, holding one row per pairing — (1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (3,3) and so on.

In ASSIGNMENT, the columns emp_id and proj_id are:
options: Foreign keys that together form a composite primary key
Secondary keys used only for retrieval
Surrogate keys generated by the DBMS
questions.explanation: Each is a foreign key on its own; together they form the composite primary key of the bridge table.

questions.question: One DIVISION operates many DEPARTMENTs; each DEPARTMENT is operated by one DIVISION. The foreign key belongs:
options: In both tables, to keep them in sync
In neither — the join works without one
questions.explanation: Many departments per division means the many side is DEPARTMENT, so division_id goes there. Putting department_id in DIVISION would only allow one department per division.

questions.question: In entity relationship modeling, an M:N relationship is valid at the conceptual level.
questions.explanation: Valid conceptually — but for the logical model and the actual ERD you need a bridge table.

questions.question: Match each SQL data definition command to its effect.

pairs.right: Creates a new table in the user's database schema
Permanently deletes a table and its data
Modifies a table definition — adds, modifies or deletes attributes or constraints
Creates a dynamic subset of rows and columns from one or more tables
Creates an index for a given table

questions.explanation: All five are DDL. Note that DROP TABLE takes the data with it — it is not a way to empty a table.

questions.question: Which pair correctly contrasts DROP TABLE with DELETE FROM?
options: DROP removes rows but keeps the table; DELETE removes the table
DROP removes the table and its data; DELETE removes rows and leaves the table in place
DROP is DML; DELETE is DDL
questions.explanation: DROP is DDL and takes the structure with it. DELETE is DML and only removes rows.

questions.question: Match each SELECT clause to the job it performs.

pairs.right: Specifies the attributes to be returned
Specifies the table(s) the data is retrieved from
Filters individual rows on the given criteria
Collects rows into groups that share values in one or more attributes
Filters the groups formed by GROUP BY
Sorts the final result rows, ascending or descending

questions.explanation: The one that trips people up is WHERE vs HAVING: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after.

questions.question: SQL's ______ clause produces a list of only unique values, removing duplicates from the result.
questions.explanation: DISTINCT. It goes immediately after SELECT: SELECT DISTINCT power_source FROM gadget;

questions.question: Match each special operator to what it tests.

pairs.right: Whether a value falls within an inclusive range
Whether a value appears in a given list
Whether text matches a pattern
Whether a value is absent altogether

questions.explanation: These four are the special operators. Note that a null is never found by = — it needs IS NULL.

questions.question: The three logical operators SQL uses to combine multiple conditions in a query are AND, OR and ______.
questions.explanation: AND, OR and NOT.

questions.question: A query reports that "Sabrina (9) reports to Sarah (1)", drawing both people from a single EMPLOYEE table. What makes this a recursive join?
options: It joins three tables at once
It joins a table to itself, because both people live in the same table
It repeats until no rows remain
questions.explanation: Both the worker and the manager are rows in the same table, so the table is joined to itself — with table aliases to tell the two copies apart.

questions.question: Match each aggregate function to what it computes.

pairs.right: How many rows there are
The total of a numeric column
The arithmetic mean of a numeric column
The smallest value
The largest value

questions.explanation: An aggregate takes a collection of rows and reduces it to a single row.

questions.question: Match each letter of CRUD to the SQL command that performs it.

pairs.right: INSERT — adds new rows
SELECT — reads and outputs rows
UPDATE — modifies existing rows
DELETE — gets rid of rows

questions.explanation: Worth memorizing: always use WHERE with UPDATE to specify which rows, and with DELETE to limit the damage.

questions.question: What happens if you run `UPDATE gadget SET daily_fee = 5;` with no WHERE clause?
options: Nothing — SQL rejects an UPDATE without WHERE
Every row in the table is changed
questions.explanation: Every row. This is exactly why you always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE.

questions.question: Write a SELECT statement that pulls all of the rows from a single field called surname in the table steward.
questions.explanation: Naming one column in the column list returns just that column, for every row.

questions.question: Write a SELECT statement that pulls all of the rows from all of the fields in the table gadget.
questions.hint: The wildcard stands in for every column.
questions.explanation: SELECT * returns every column of every row.

questions.question: List the locality_name values from the locality table that do NOT end with a vowel (a, e, i, o, u). Your result cannot contain duplicates. Sort by locality_name.
questions.hint: Either test the last character with right(name, 1), or chain NOT LIKE '%a' … for each vowel. Careful: y is not a vowel here.
questions.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT locality_name
FROM locality
WHERE right(locality_name, 1) NOT IN ('a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u')
ORDER BY locality_name;
questions.explanation: Both approaches work. The trap is names ending in y — Alder Bay and Bellamy both belong in the result, because y is not on the vowel list.

questions.question: For every patron, output surname and given_name, plus a derived column that joins given_name and surname with a single space between them. Use the concat(field1, field2, …) function and alias the derived column as full_name. Sort by surname, then by given_name.
questions.hint: concat() takes as many arguments as you give it, so the space can be one of them. Name the derived column with AS.
questions.solution:
SELECT surname,
       given_name,
       concat(given_name, ' ', surname) AS full_name
FROM patron
ORDER BY surname, given_name;
questions.explanation: A derived column is computed rather than stored. The AS alias gives it a usable name in the result — without it the header is the whole expression.

questions.question: Return hourly_rate, surname, branch_label and locality_name for every steward, sorted by hourly_rate from largest to smallest, with ties broken by surname. branch_label is in the branch table and locality_name is in the locality table; the common keys are branch_id and locality_id.
questions.hint: Two joins in a row. Because the key names match on both sides, JOIN … USING (key) works.
questions.solution:
SELECT s.hourly_rate, s.surname, b.branch_label, l.locality_name
FROM steward s
INNER JOIN branch b USING (branch_id)
INNER JOIN locality l USING (locality_id)
ORDER BY s.hourly_rate DESC, s.surname;
questions.explanation: Joins chain: steward reaches branch by branch_id, and branch reaches locality by locality_id. A steward has no locality_id of its own — you have to hop through branch.

questions.question: List the gadget_title of every gadget in the group whose group_label is 'Plumbing'. You must filter on the actual group label, not the id. This needs three tables — gadget, gadget_group_map and gadget_group — joined on gadget_id and group_id.
questions.hint: gadget_group_map is the bridge table resolving the M:N between gadgets and groups. You have to pass through it.
questions.solution:
SELECT gadget_title
FROM gadget
INNER JOIN gadget_group_map USING (gadget_id)
INNER JOIN gadget_group USING (group_id)
WHERE gadget_group.group_label = 'Plumbing';
questions.explanation: This is the classic three-table pattern for an M:N relationship: the two entity tables plus the bridge between them. There is no direct link from gadget to gadget_group.

questions.question: List the unique given_name and surname of every patron who took out a loan between '2024-06-01' and '2024-08-31'. Sort by surname, then given_name. Use the DISTINCT keyword to eliminate duplicates. The common key is patron_id.
questions.hint: A patron who borrowed four times would otherwise appear four times.
questions.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT given_name, surname
FROM checkout
INNER JOIN patron USING (patron_id)
WHERE checked_out_on BETWEEN '2024-06-01' AND '2024-08-31'
ORDER BY surname, given_name;
questions.explanation: Joining to a table on the many side multiplies rows. DISTINCT collapses them back down to one per patron.

questions.question: List the surname of every patron together with the score_pct of any safety course result above 75. Sort by the last three characters of the surname; where two rows tie on those three characters, sort by result_id.
questions.hint: right(text, 3) returns the last three characters. You can sort by an expression, not just a column.
questions.solution:
SELECT p.surname, r.score_pct
FROM course_result r
INNER JOIN patron p USING (patron_id)
WHERE r.score_pct > 75
ORDER BY right(p.surname, 3), r.result_id;
questions.explanation: ORDER BY accepts any expression. The secondary sort on result_id is what makes the order fully determined when several surnames end the same way.

questions.question:
Crow's Foot notation marks each end of a relationship line with one of six connectors, built from a circle, a bar, and a crow's foot.

A = crow's foot only
B = bar + crow's foot
C = circle + crow's foot
D = single bar
E = double bar
F = circle + bar

Match each connector to what it means.

pairs.right: Many
One or many (mandatory, many)
Zero or many (optional, many)
One
One and only one (mandatory, exactly one)
Zero or one (optional, at most one)

questions.explanation: Read each connector as two symbols: the outer one is the minimum, the inner one is the maximum. A circle means zero (optional), a bar means one, and a crow's foot means many.

questions.question: In Crow's Foot notation, what does a circle on a relationship line always add?
options: That the participation is optional — the minimum is zero
That the attribute is a primary key
questions.explanation: Circle = zero = optional participation. A bar = one, and a crow's foot = many.

questions.question: A relationship in which an entity does not have to participate — the minimum cardinality is zero — is called ______ participation.
questions.explanation: Optional participation, drawn with a circle. Mandatory participation requires at least one related row, and is drawn with a bar.

questions.question: On a completed ERD, an attribute name shown in bold and underlined at the top of the entity box represents the:
questions.explanation: Primary key attributes are listed first and marked bold and underlined, above the dividing line in the entity box.

questions.question: On a completed ERD, an attribute name shown in italics below the dividing line typically represents a ______ key.
questions.explanation: Foreign key attributes are italicized, distinguishing them from the primary key and from plain descriptive attributes.

questions.question:
An ERD shows an entity box laid out like this:

    row 1:  P1 | **P2**   (bold, underlined)
    row 2:  P3 | *P4*     (italic)
    row 3:  P5 (one or more fields)

What belongs in slot P1?
options: The marker PK, labelling the row beside it as the primary key
questions.explanation: The narrow left-hand cells hold the key markers: PK beside the primary key row, FK beside the foreign key row. The entity name sits in the header above the box.

questions.question:
An ERD shows an entity box laid out like this:

    row 1:  P1 | **P2**   (bold, underlined)
    row 2:  P3 | *P4*     (italic)
    row 3:  P5 (one or more fields)

What belongs in slot P3?
questions.explanation: P3 is the marker cell for the italicized attribute beside it, so it holds FK.

questions.question:
Business rules: "A DEPOT must store at least one CRATE, and can store many. Every CRATE must be stored at exactly one DEPOT."

Legend: A = crow's foot; B = bar + crow's foot; C = circle + crow's foot; D = single bar; E = double bar; F = circle + bar.

Reading from CRATE toward DEPOT, which connector belongs on the DEPOT end of the line?
questions.explanation: Each crate must be at exactly one depot: mandatory, and no more than one. That's the double bar, E.

questions.question:
Business rules: "A DEPOT must store at least one CRATE, and can store many. Every CRATE must be stored at exactly one DEPOT."

Legend: A = crow's foot; B = bar + crow's foot; C = circle + crow's foot; D = single bar; E = double bar; F = circle + bar.

Reading from DEPOT toward CRATE, which connector belongs on the CRATE end of the line?
questions.explanation: "Must store at least one" makes it mandatory, and "can store many" makes the maximum many — bar plus crow's foot, connector B.

questions.question:
Business rule: "Some technicians, known as 'floaters', are not assigned to any WORKSHOP."

Legend: A = crow's foot; B = bar + crow's foot; C = circle + crow's foot; D = single bar; E = double bar; F = circle + bar.

Each technician who IS assigned belongs to just one workshop. Which connector belongs on the WORKSHOP end of the TECHNICIAN–WORKSHOP line?
questions.explanation: A floater has no workshop, so the minimum is zero (circle); an assigned technician has just one, so the maximum is one (bar). Circle + bar is connector F.

questions.question: On an ERD, where does the foreign key go for a 1:M relationship between LEAGUE (1) and TEAM (M)?
options: In LEAGUE, referencing TEAM's primary key
In TEAM, referencing LEAGUE's primary key
Foreign keys aren't needed for 1:M relationships
questions.explanation: The foreign key always goes on the many side, referencing the primary key on the one side.

questions.question: Business rule: "A VOLUNTEER can sign up for many SHIFTs, and each SHIFT can be covered by many VOLUNTEERs." How should this be modeled?
options: Put a foreign key in VOLUNTEER
Put a foreign key in SHIFT
Create a composite/bridge entity holding both primary keys as foreign keys
Merge VOLUNTEER and SHIFT into one table
questions.explanation: M:N relationships need a bridge (associative) entity containing both related primary keys as foreign keys.

questions.question:
Business rule: "A VOLUNTEER can sign up for many SHIFTs, and each SHIFT can be covered by many VOLUNTEERs."

This M:N is resolved with a bridge entity, SIGNUP. It would most likely use a ______ primary key made up of volunteer_id and shift_id together.
questions.explanation: A bridge entity's primary key is typically a composite key formed from the two foreign keys it holds.

questions.question: Business rules: "One of the STEWARDs manages each BRANCH, and each BRANCH is managed by only one STEWARD." What kind of relationship is this?
questions.explanation: One manager per branch and one branch per manager makes it 1:1. Note this is separate from the 1:M relationship recording which branch each steward works at.

questions.question: How is a recursive 1:M relationship — each STEWARD is supervised by one other STEWARD — implemented in the table itself?
options: With a second copy of the table
With a foreign key column in STEWARD that references STEWARD's own primary key
questions.explanation: supervisor_id sits in STEWARD and references steward_id in the same table. The top of the hierarchy has a null there.

questions.question:
Business rules: "A TEAM may or may not have a PLAYER. A PLAYER must have a TEAM. A TEAM may have many PLAYERs. A PLAYER has only one TEAM."

Legend: A = crow's foot; B = bar + crow's foot; C = circle + crow's foot; D = single bar; E = double bar; F = circle + bar.

Which connector belongs on the PLAYER end?
questions.explanation: "May or may not have a PLAYER" makes the minimum zero, and "may have many" makes the maximum many — circle plus crow's foot, C.

questions.question:
Business rules: "A TEAM may or may not have a PLAYER. A PLAYER must have a TEAM. A TEAM may have many PLAYERs. A PLAYER has only one TEAM."

Legend: A = crow's foot; B = bar + crow's foot; C = circle + crow's foot; D = single bar; E = double bar; F = circle + bar.

Which connector belongs on the TEAM end?
questions.explanation: "A PLAYER must have a TEAM" and "has only one TEAM": mandatory and exactly one, so the double bar, E.

questions.question: Business rules: "A PLAYER must have a PARENT. A PARENT must have a PLAYER. A PLAYER may have many PARENTs. A PARENT may have many PLAYERs." What does the ERD need?
options: A bridge entity between PLAYER and PARENT
questions.explanation: Many on both sides is M:N, so it needs a bridge entity holding player_id and parent_id.

questions.question: Match each business-rule phrase to the cardinality pair it establishes at that end of the line.

pairs.right: (1,1) — mandatory one

pairs.left: "must have at least one, and may have many"
pairs.right: (1,many) — mandatory many

pairs.left: "may or may not have one or more"
pairs.right: (0,many) — optional many
(0,1) — optional one

questions.explanation: Every connector is a (minimum, maximum) pair. Find the two numbers in the sentence and the symbol follows.

questions.question: An ERD models COURSE and CLASS, where one COURSE is offered as many CLASS sections and each CLASS belongs to one COURSE. Which is the correct key arrangement?
options: class_id is the primary key of CLASS, and course_id appears in CLASS as a foreign key
course_id is the primary key of CLASS
class_id appears in COURSE as a foreign key
The two tables share a single primary key
questions.explanation: CLASS is the many side, so it keeps its own primary key and carries course_id as a foreign key.

questions.question:
Business rules for a delivery firm:
 • A DEPOT employs many DRIVERs, but each DRIVER is employed by one DEPOT.
 • Some drivers, known as "relief" drivers, are not assigned to any depot.
 • A DRIVER may be assigned many ROUTEs, and a ROUTE may have many DRIVERs assigned to it.
 • A ROUTE must have at least one DRIVER assigned.

List the tables you would create and the key columns in each.
questions.modelAnswer:
DEPOT — primary key depot_id.

DRIVER — primary key driver_id, plus depot_id as a foreign key to DEPOT. It must allow nulls, because a relief driver has no depot.

ROUTE — primary key route_id.

DRIVER_ROUTE (bridge entity) — driver_id and route_id, each a foreign key, together forming the composite primary key. This is what resolves the M:N between DRIVER and ROUTE.

Connectors: on the DEPOT–DRIVER line, the DEPOT end is optional-one (circle + bar, F) because of the relief drivers, and the DRIVER end is optional-many (circle + crow's foot, C). On ROUTE–DRIVER_ROUTE the ROUTE end is mandatory-one (E) and the bridge end is mandatory-many (B), since a route must have at least one driver.
rubric: Created four tables, including a bridge between DRIVER and ROUTE
Put depot_id in DRIVER (the many side), not driver_id in DEPOT
Noted that depot_id must allow nulls because of the relief drivers
Gave the bridge a composite primary key of the two foreign keys
questions.explanation: Two habits carry most ERD questions: put the foreign key on the many side, and reach for a bridge table the moment you read "many … many".

questions.question: ______ is the process of evaluating and correcting table structures to minimize data redundancies.
questions.explanation: Normalization. Reducing redundancy is what reduces the update, insertion and deletion anomalies.

questions.question: Match each normal form to its defining characteristic.

pairs.right: Table format, no repeating groups, and the primary key is identified
In 1NF and no partial dependencies
In 2NF and no transitive dependencies
Every determinant is a candidate key
In 3NF and no independent multivalued dependencies

questions.explanation: Each form builds on the one before it. Memorizing "1NF, then kill partial, then kill transitive" gets you through most of a normalization problem.

questions.question: All valid relational tables satisfy the 1NF requirements.
questions.explanation: If a table isn't in 1NF, it isn't really a relational table.

questions.question: Going from 1NF to 2NF removes ______ dependencies.
questions.explanation: Partial dependencies — where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key.

questions.question: Going from 2NF to 3NF removes ______ dependencies.
questions.explanation: Transitive dependencies — where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute.

questions.question: "Attribute B is fully functionally dependent on attribute A if each value of A determines one and only one value of B." This defines:
questions.explanation: Functional dependence. Written PROJ_NUM → PROJ_NAME and read "PROJ_NUM functionally determines PROJ_NAME".

questions.question: A table whose primary key is a single attribute can still contain a partial dependency.
questions.explanation: A partial dependency needs a determinant that is part of the key. With a one-column key there is no part to depend on, so any 1NF table with a simple key is automatically in 2NF.

questions.question: More tables require more I/O operations and processing logic to join them.
questions.explanation: Which is why it also says normalization is important, but only part of the design process.

questions.question:
CATERING_ORDER is in 1NF with the following columns:

  booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city,
  dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price, portions

The primary key is booking_ref + dish_code.

Write the complete dependency set for the table as it stands in 1NF — the full dependency on the whole key, every partial dependency, and every transitive dependency.
questions.modelAnswer:
Full functional dependency on the whole primary key:
  (booking_ref, dish_code) → portions

Partial dependencies:
  booking_ref → booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city
  dish_code   → dish_name, dish_style, dish_price

Transitive dependency:
  client_no → client_name, client_city

Read it as: how many portions were ordered needs both halves of the key; everything about the booking follows from booking_ref alone; everything about the dish follows from dish_code alone; and the client's name and city follow from client_no, which is itself just an ordinary attribute of the booking.
rubric: Identified (booking_ref, dish_code) → portions as the only full dependency on the whole key
Listed booking_ref → booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city as a partial dependency
Listed dish_code → dish_name, dish_style, dish_price as a partial dependency
Identified client_no → client_name, client_city as the transitive dependency
questions.explanation: Work in this order every time: what needs the whole key, what needs only part of it, and what hangs off a non-key attribute. That ordering is the dependency set.

questions.question:
CATERING_ORDER is in 1NF with the following columns:

  booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city,
  dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price, portions

The primary key is booking_ref + dish_code.

Write the 2NF relational schemas — the tables you get after removing the partial dependencies. Underline or otherwise mark the primary key of each.
questions.modelAnswer:
BOOKING (booking_ref [PK], booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city)

DISH (dish_code [PK], dish_name, dish_style, dish_price)

BOOKING_LINE (booking_ref [PK, FK], dish_code [PK, FK], portions)

Each partial dependency became its own table, keyed on its determinant. What remains in BOOKING_LINE is the original composite key plus the one attribute that genuinely needed both halves of it — portions. The two key columns are now foreign keys back to BOOKING and DISH.

This is 2NF, not yet 3NF: BOOKING still carries the transitive dependency client_no → client_name, client_city.
rubric: Produced three tables
Keyed BOOKING on booking_ref and DISH on dish_code
Kept portions in the linking table with the composite key (booking_ref, dish_code)
Marked the composite key columns as foreign keys as well as the primary key
Noted that this is still only 2NF because a transitive dependency remains
questions.explanation: The mechanical rule: each partial dependency's determinant becomes a new table's primary key, and everything it determined goes with it.

questions.question:
CATERING_ORDER is in 1NF with the following columns:

  booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city,
  dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price, portions

The primary key is booking_ref + dish_code.

Take it all the way to 3NF. Write the 3NF relational schemas, marking the primary key and any foreign keys in each table.
questions.modelAnswer:
CLIENT (client_no [PK], client_name, client_city)

BOOKING (booking_ref [PK], booking_date, client_no [FK to CLIENT])

DISH (dish_code [PK], dish_name, dish_style, dish_price)

BOOKING_LINE (booking_ref [PK, FK to BOOKING], dish_code [PK, FK to DISH], portions)

The move from 2NF to 3NF was the first two tables: the transitive dependency client_no → client_name, client_city came out of BOOKING into its own CLIENT table, and client_no stayed behind in BOOKING as the foreign key linking them.

Now every non-key attribute in every table depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
rubric: Produced four tables
Created CLIENT keyed on client_no, holding client_name and client_city
Left client_no in BOOKING as a foreign key
Left DISH and BOOKING_LINE unchanged from 2NF
Marked primary and foreign keys throughout
questions.explanation: "The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key" is a compact test: nothing but the key catches transitive dependencies, and the whole key catches partial ones.

questions.question:
SEMINAR_ROSTER is in 1NF:

  seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity,
  attendee_id, attendee_name, attendee_email, grade

The primary key is seminar_code + attendee_id. Each seminar meets in exactly one room.

Write the complete dependency set for this table in 1NF.
questions.modelAnswer:
Full functional dependency on the whole primary key:
  (seminar_code, attendee_id) → grade

Partial dependencies:
  seminar_code → seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity
  attendee_id  → attendee_name, attendee_email

Transitive dependency:
  room_code → room_capacity

Only the grade needs both halves of the key: it is one person's mark in one seminar. Room capacity is listed twice above deliberately — it follows from seminar_code by way of room_code, and the room_code → room_capacity link is what makes it transitive.
rubric: Identified (seminar_code, attendee_id) → grade as the only full dependency
Listed seminar_code → seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity
Listed attendee_id → attendee_name, attendee_email
Identified room_code → room_capacity as the transitive dependency
questions.explanation: Two partial dependencies, one from each half of the composite key, plus one transitive dependency hanging off a nonprime attribute — the same shape as the catering example.

questions.question: Write the 3NF relational schemas for SEMINAR_ROSTER (seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity, attendee_id, attendee_name, attendee_email, grade), primary key seminar_code + attendee_id, where each seminar meets in exactly one room.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROOM (room_code [PK], room_capacity)

SEMINAR (seminar_code [PK], seminar_title, room_code [FK to ROOM])

ATTENDEE (attendee_id [PK], attendee_name, attendee_email)

ENROLLMENT (seminar_code [PK, FK to SEMINAR], attendee_id [PK, FK to ATTENDEE], grade)

The two partial dependencies became SEMINAR and ATTENDEE; the transitive dependency became ROOM, with room_code left behind in SEMINAR as the foreign key. ENROLLMENT keeps the composite key and the single attribute that needed all of it.

ENROLLMENT is a bridge table — the M:N between seminars and attendees, resolved.
rubric: Produced four tables
Split ROOM out with room_code as its primary key
Left room_code in SEMINAR as a foreign key
Kept grade in a linking table keyed on (seminar_code, attendee_id)
Marked both linking columns as foreign keys
questions.explanation: Worth noticing: normalizing an M:N-shaped table produces exactly the bridge entity you would have drawn on the ERD. The two techniques agree.
